title: Lesson 10 - A2.1.3 Software Vulnerabilities
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How can software weaknesses put people and organisations at risk?

sections.heading: What is a software vulnerability?
sections.text: A software vulnerability is a weakness or flaw in software that could be exploited to cause harm, steal data or gain unauthorised access.
points: Example: a student installs software from an untrustworthy website. The installer contains malware, giving an attacker a way into the device
Poor software design: security wasn't properly considered when the software was made
Operating system choices: an unsuitable or poorly secured operating system increases risk
Poor user habits: unsafe choices, such as downloading from untrusted sources
Poor checking and testing: software and third-party providers aren't checked or tested properly

sections.heading: Downloading software safely
sections.text: Software from an untrusted source may contain security flaws, malware or other malicious content. Before installing, check:

head: Check
What to do
rows: Download from a reliable, official source, not a random download site
Make sure the download page uses HTTPS and shows the padlock (the connection is encrypted)
Check the website's certificate is valid
Scan the software before installing it
Check the hash to make sure the file hasn't been changed or tampered with

sections.heading: Hash checks
sections.text: A hash value is like a digital fingerprint for a file. If even one letter in the file changes, the hash becomes completely different, so a hash check shows whether a file has been changed or tampered with.

head: Step
What to do
rows: On the official website, find the hash value provided (often SHA-256) and copy it
On Windows, open Command Prompt and type: certutil -hashfile [file path] SHA256
If they match exactly, the file is safe. If not, don't install or open it: it may be corrupted or hacked

sections.heading: Illegal copies and zero-day exploits
points: Illegal or unofficial copies may not get important security updates or patches
If the copy has been tampered with, it could contain malware or a backdoor, giving attackers a way in
A zero-day exploit uses a security flaw that was previously unknown
Once it's discovered, the manufacturer must release a patch quickly
Until then there's no fix, so the longer the patch takes, the more time criminals have to exploit it

sections.heading: Outdated software
points: Software that isn't regularly updated becomes vulnerable to new threats
Security patches fix known weaknesses and protect systems from attackers
Link to Lesson 9: one unpatched device can be the weak link into a whole network

sections.heading: SQL injection
sections.text: SQL (Structured Query Language) is how websites and apps talk to databases, e.g. to log users in, display products and find information. SQL injection is an attack where a hacker inserts ('injects') malicious SQL code into a website's input fields, trying to trick the system into giving them access to the database.
points: Targets: login boxes, search bars and online forms
If the input isn't properly protected, attackers can bypass login screens; view usernames, passwords or bank details; change or delete data; reach admin controls; and steal personal or customer data
Why it's serious: data breaches, whole databases deleted, privacy, financial and legal problems, including breaking GDPR

sections.heading: How SQL injection happens: the login example
sections.text: The website logs users in with: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = input AND password = input. Normally someone types Username: Alex, Password: password123. The attacker instead types: ' OR 1=1 --
points: The ' (quote mark) ends the username text early, so what follows is treated as part of the SQL command
OR 1=1 adds a condition that is always true (1 always equals 1)
-- turns the rest of the line into a comment, so the password check is ignored
Result: the database answers 'yes' without a correct username or password, and the attacker gets in

Standard ways to prevent it (not on the slides): validate and check all input, use parameterised queries so input is never treated as code, and give the website's database account only the access it needs

diagram.alt: Top: a normal login query checks WHERE username equals Alex AND password equals password123, so you only get in with the right password. Bottom: the attacker types quote OR 1=1 dash dash as the username. The quote ends the username text, OR 1=1 is always true, and the two dashes turn the rest of the line, including the password check, into a comment. Result: logged in without a valid password.
diagram.caption: Each part of the attack input changes what the database is asked to do.

sections.heading: Case study: Google Chrome zero-day (2022)
sections.text: In March 2022, hackers from North Korea found a zero-day weakness in the Google Chrome browser.
points: They used phishing emails to take users to a fake website
The Chrome vulnerability was used to install spyware and remote monitoring software. It's still unclear what data was taken
Google issued an emergency patch
Lessons: even trusted software can have vulnerabilities; browsers are common targets because so many people use them; patches reduce the risk once a flaw is found

sections.heading: Research task: a real software vulnerability
sections.text: Choose one: the Chrome zero-day, WannaCry and unpatched Windows, a real SQL injection attack (e.g. TalkTalk, Lesson 8), or a vulnerability in a popular app. Answer these five questions and say where you found the information:
points: 1. What software or system was affected?
2. What was the vulnerability?
3. How was it exploited?
4. What was the impact?
5. How was it fixed or reduced?
Challenge: which security measure could have reduced the risk? Explain why

keyIdea: Software vulnerabilities come from poor design, poor choices and poor habits. Attackers exploit untrusted downloads, illegal copies, zero-days, outdated software and unprotected input fields (SQL injection), so download safely, check hashes, patch quickly and protect databases.
flashcards: Software vulnerability
A weakness or flaw in software that could be exploited to cause harm, steal data or gain unauthorised access.
Four causes of software vulnerabilities
Poor software design, operating system choices, poor user habits, poor checking and testing.
Trusted source
A reliable, official place to download software, e.g. the developer's own website.
HTTPS and padlock
Shows the connection to the website is encrypted. Check for it before downloading.
Website certificate
A digital certificate proving a site's identity. It should be valid before you download.
Hash value
A file's 'digital fingerprint'. Change even one letter and it becomes completely different.
Hash check
Comparing the official hash with your file's hash. A match means the file hasn't been tampered with.
SHA-256
A common hashing method used to create hash values for downloads.
certutil
Windows command to calculate a file's hash: certutil -hashfile [file path] SHA256.
Illegal copy of software
Unofficial software that may miss security updates and could contain malware or a backdoor.
Backdoor
A hidden way into a system that lets attackers bypass normal security.
Zero-day exploit
An attack using a previously unknown flaw. No patch exists yet, so it's especially risky.
Patch
A fix released by the manufacturer to correct a known weakness.
Outdated software
Software not regularly updated, so it's vulnerable to new threats.
SQL
Structured Query Language: how websites and apps communicate with databases.
SQL injection
Inserting malicious SQL code into input fields (login, search, forms) to trick the system into giving database access.
A classic SQL injection: ' ends the input, OR 1=1 is always true, -- comments out the password check.
Input field
A place users type into, such as login boxes, search bars and online forms.
What SQL injection can do
Bypass logins; view, change or delete data; reach admin controls; steal customer data.
SQL injection and GDPR
Leaking personal data through SQL injection can break privacy laws like GDPR.
Parameterised query
A safe way to build database queries so user input is never run as code (standard prevention).
Chrome zero-day (2022)
North Korean hackers used phishing and an unknown Chrome flaw to install spyware; Google issued an emergency patch.

o: A weakness or flaw in software that could be exploited
quiz.e: It can be exploited to cause harm, steal data or gain unauthorised access.

quiz.q: Which is the safer place to download software?
o: A link in an unexpected email
quiz.e: Official sources are trusted. Random sites may bundle malware.

quiz.q: What does HTTPS and the padlock tell you about a website connection?
quiz.e: It shows the connection is secure (encrypted). You should still check the source, certificate and hash.

quiz.q: What does a hash check confirm?
o: The file is the newest version
The file hasn't been changed or tampered with
quiz.e: If the hashes match exactly, the file is the same as the official one.

quiz.q: You calculate a file's hash and it doesn't match the one on the official website. What should you do?
quiz.e: A mismatch means the file may be corrupted or hacked.

quiz.q: Which Windows command calculates a file's SHA-256 hash?
Why might an illegal copy of software be a security risk?
o: It may not get security updates and could contain malware or a backdoor
quiz.e: Tampered, unpatched copies give attackers a way in.

quiz.q: A software flaw is discovered but no patch has been released yet. Why is this especially risky?
o: Because there's no fix yet, so attackers can exploit it freely
quiz.e: That's a zero-day: the longer the patch takes, the longer criminals have.

quiz.q: A company has an internet-facing database with poor input checking. What attack should it worry about?
quiz.e: Unprotected input fields connected to a database invite SQL injection.
Structured Query Language: how sites and apps talk to databases.

quiz.q: In the attack input ' OR 1=1 --, what does OR 1=1 do?
o: Adds a condition that is always true
quiz.e: 1 always equals 1, so the check always passes.

quiz.q: In ' OR 1=1 --, what do the two dashes (--) do?
o: Turn the rest of the command into a comment, so the password check is ignored
quiz.e: Everything after -- is ignored, including the password part.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a cause of software vulnerabilities listed on the slides?
quiz.e: The four causes: poor design, OS choices, poor user habits, poor checking/testing.

quiz.q: In the 2022 Chrome zero-day, how were users taken to the fake website?
quiz.e: Hackers used phishing emails, then exploited the Chrome flaw to install spyware.

quiz.q: Why are web browsers common targets?
quiz.e: A single browser flaw can reach a huge number of people.

quiz.q: Which law could an organisation break if SQL injection leaks customers' personal data?
quiz.e: Your slides list breaking privacy laws such as GDPR as a consequence.

apply.title: Spot the software risk
apply.intro: Read each situation and pick the vulnerability, or the best check or fix.

items.task: A student downloads a 'free' version of expensive editing software from a random website.
items.e: Untrusted and probably illegal: it could contain malware or a backdoor and won't get updates.

items.task: Before installing a program, you want to be sure the file is exactly the official one. What should you do?
o: Do a hash check and compare it with the official hash
items.e: Matching hashes prove the file hasn't been tampered with.

items.task: An attacker types ' OR 1=1 -- into a website's username box and gets logged in.
items.e: Malicious SQL in an input field is SQL injection.

items.task: Hackers exploit a browser flaw that nobody, not even the maker, knew about. No patch exists yet.
items.e: A previously unknown flaw with no patch is a zero-day.

items.task: A company's PCs still run software that hasn't been updated in two years.
items.e: Missing patches leave known weaknesses open.

items.task: A download page has no padlock and the browser says 'Not secure'. What should you do?
o: Don't download; find the official, HTTPS source instead
items.e: Check HTTPS, the padlock and a valid certificate before downloading.

items.task: A web form lets users search the product database, and nothing checks what they type. What's the main risk?
items.e: Unchecked input fields connected to a database can be used for SQL injection.

items.task: Software is designed without anyone thinking about security until after it's released. Which cause of vulnerabilities is this?
items.e: Security wasn't considered properly when it was created.

items.task: A third-party app is added to a company's system without anyone testing it.
items.e: Software and third-party providers should be checked and tested.

items.task: Google releases an emergency Chrome update after a zero-day is found. What should users do?
items.e: Patches close the vulnerability once it's discovered.

items.task: Which is the BEST way for a developer to stop SQL injection?
o: Validate input and use parameterised queries
items.e: Checking input and never running it as code stops injection (standard practice).

items.task: A file's hash from your computer is: 9a3f…. The website shows: 9a3f… with exactly the same characters. What does this mean?
o: The file is safe: it hasn't been changed
items.e: An exact match means the file is the same as the official one.

pts: A weakness or flaw in software
that could be exploited to cause harm, steal data or gain unauthorised access
exam.tip: Weakness + what an attacker could do with it.

exam.q: 2. Describe three checks a user should make before installing downloaded software.
pts: Any one: download from a trusted, official source
A second: check the page uses HTTPS with the padlock and has a valid certificate
A third: scan it for malware / do a hash check to make sure it hasn't been tampered with
exam.tip: Your slides list five checks. Any three, each described clearly.

exam.q: 3. Explain how a hash check shows that a downloaded file has not been tampered with.
pts: The official website provides the file's original hash value (a digital fingerprint, e.g. SHA-256)
The user calculates the hash of the downloaded file, e.g. using certutil
If the two match exactly the file is unchanged; if even one character of the file changed, the hash would be completely different
exam.tip: Get the hash → calculate yours → compare. Explain WHY a match proves it's unchanged.

exam.q: 4. A software flaw is discovered but the manufacturer has not released a patch yet. Explain why this is especially risky.
pts: This is a zero-day: the flaw was previously unknown
There is no patch yet, so systems can't be protected by updating
The longer it takes to release a patch, the more time criminals have to exploit it
exam.tip: Name it (zero-day), then explain the time window.

exam.q: 5. Explain why an illegal copy of software is a security risk.
pts: It may not receive important security updates or patches, and could have been tampered with
so it might contain malware or a backdoor that gives attackers a way into the system

exam.sc: Brightside Pharmacy lets customers order prescriptions on its website, which has a login page and a search box connected to a customer database. The website's server software hasn't been updated for 18 months. Staff PCs run an illegal 'cracked' copy of a design program, and staff often download free tools from whichever site comes up first in a search.
exam.q: 6. Identify the type of attack Brightside Pharmacy's website is most at risk from.
pts: SQL injection
exam.tip: Clue: a login page and search box connected to a database.

exam.sc: Brightside Pharmacy lets customers order prescriptions on its website, which has a login page and a search box connected to a customer database. The website's server software hasn't been updated for 18 months. Staff PCs run an illegal 'cracked' copy of a design program, and staff often download free tools from whichever site comes up first in a search.
exam.q: 7. Explain how an attacker could use SQL injection on Brightside Pharmacy's login page.
pts: The attacker types malicious SQL code into the login box instead of a username, e.g. ' OR 1=1 --
If the input isn't protected, the database treats it as part of the SQL command: OR 1=1 is always true and -- removes the password check
so the attacker is logged in without a valid password and can reach the customer database
exam.tip: Show you understand HOW the code tricks the database, not just that it does.

exam.sc: Brightside Pharmacy lets customers order prescriptions on its website, which has a login page and a search box connected to a customer database. The website's server software hasn't been updated for 18 months. Staff PCs run an illegal 'cracked' copy of a design program, and staff often download free tools from whichever site comes up first in a search.
exam.q: 8. Explain two impacts of a successful SQL injection attack on Brightside Pharmacy.
pts: Impact 1, e.g. a data breach: customers' personal and prescription details are viewed or stolen
which could break GDPR and lead to fines and legal problems
Impact 2, e.g. data changed or deleted, such as prescription records
so orders go wrong or are lost, causing financial problems and damage to trust
exam.tip: Use the slides' list: breaches, deleted databases, privacy, financial and legal problems. Link to medical data.

exam.sc: Brightside Pharmacy lets customers order prescriptions on its website, which has a login page and a search box connected to a customer database. The website's server software hasn't been updated for 18 months. Staff PCs run an illegal 'cracked' copy of a design program, and staff often download free tools from whichever site comes up first in a search.
exam.q: 9. Evaluate the measures Brightside Pharmacy could take to reduce its software vulnerabilities.
pts: Update/patch the website's server software: closes 18 months of known weaknesses
Protect the website's input fields (validation, parameterised queries) to stop SQL injection
Replace the cracked design program with a legal, licensed copy that gets updates and has no hidden backdoor
Safe download rules: official sources only, HTTPS and certificate checks, malware scans and hash checks
Limitations: patches can't stop zero-days, and rules only work if staff follow them, so training is needed
Justified conclusion: which measure is most urgent (e.g. fixing the internet-facing website, as it holds medical data) and why
exam.tip: Top-grade "evaluate" = several measures linked to Brightside's actual problems, their limits, and a clear priority.
